A series of appropriations limits on U.S. support for the Contras fighting Nicaragua's government. The first, in December 1982 (in Pub. L. 97-377), barred funds for the purpose of overthrowing that government. The strictest, Sec. 8066 of Pub. L. 98-473 (October 1984), barred the CIA, the Defense Department, and any other agency involved in intelligence activities from spending funds during fiscal year 1985 to support military or paramilitary operations in Nicaragua, directly or indirectly.

::: {.official-links}
**Read the law** (official GovInfo text)

[Enacted text: 98 Stat. 1935](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/statute/98/1935){.btn-official}
:::

## Key provisions

- Sec. 8066(a) (FY1985): no funds available to the CIA, the Defense Department, or any intelligence entity for direct or indirect support of military or paramilitary operations in Nicaragua.
- Sec. 8066(b): the bar could lift after February 28, 1985 only on a presidential report and a joint resolution approving further support.
- Named for Representative Edward Boland, then chairman of the House intelligence committee.

## Why it matters

The Boland Amendments show the purse used against intelligence activity rather than open war. Efforts to keep supporting the Contras outside appropriated channels led to the Iran-Contra affair, which in turn led Congress to write the statutory definition of covert action and tighten finding and notice rules in 1991 (see the [National Security Act](nsa-1947.qmd) and the [Intel Oversight Act](intel-oversight-1980.qmd)). They are a standing reference point whenever a funding limit is proposed for an intelligence or special operations activity.

## Current status

The amendments were annual appropriations limits for fiscal years 1983 through 1985 and are no longer operative. Of historical and precedential interest.

[Last checked November 24, 2026.]{.checked}
